title: The Eiffel Tower: Location, History and Engineering
text: The Eiffel Tower is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It was designed by engineer Gustave Eiffel's company and completed in 1889 for the Exposition Universelle, a world's fair held to celebrate the centennial of the French Revolution. The structure was initially criticized by some artists, but it became a defining symbol of Paris and French engineering. Today it is visited by millions of people each year, and its observation platforms provide views across the city. The tower's height changes slightly with temperature as the iron expands and contracts.

title: Boiling Point of Water at Standard Pressure
text: At sea level, pure water boils at approximately 100 degrees Celsius, or 212 degrees Fahrenheit. Boiling occurs when the vapor pressure of the liquid equals the pressure exerted by the surrounding atmosphere, allowing bubbles of water vapor to form throughout the liquid. The boiling point decreases at high elevations because atmospheric pressure is lower and increases in a pressure cooker because pressure is higher. Dissolved substances can also alter the boiling point. These principles are important in cooking, sterilization, and industrial heat-transfer systems.

title: Canberra and the Australian Capital Territory
text: Canberra is the capital city of Australia and the seat of the country's federal government. It is located in the Australian Capital Territory between Sydney and Melbourne, whose rivalry influenced the decision to establish a separate inland capital. The city was planned after an international design competition won by Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. Canberra contains Parliament House, the High Court, national museums, galleries, and major public institutions. Its layout includes broad avenues, planned suburbs, and parkland around Lake Burley Griffin.

title: Photosynthesis: Conversion of Light to Chemical Energy
text: Photosynthesis is the biological process through which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy. In green plants, chlorophyll absorbs light in chloroplasts, and that energy drives reactions that split water molecules and capture carbon dioxide. The resulting sugars support growth and cellular respiration, while oxygen is released as a by-product. Photosynthesis is commonly summarized as carbon dioxide plus water producing glucose and oxygen in the presence of light. It supports nearly every food web and supplies much of the atmosphere's oxygen.

title: The Pacific Ocean: Scale, Depth and Geography
text: The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions. It extends from the Arctic Ocean to the Southern Ocean and lies between Asia and Australia in the west and the Americas in the east. The Pacific contains thousands of volcanic and coral islands across Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia. The Mariana Trench, the deepest known oceanic trench, is in the western Pacific. Its currents, tectonic boundaries, fisheries, and climate patterns make the ocean important to science, trade, and coastal communities.

title: Paris Landmarks and the Champ de Mars
text: The Champ de Mars is a large public green space in the seventh arrondissement of Paris, extending northwest from the Ecole Militaire toward the Eiffel Tower. The park has hosted national celebrations, exhibitions, concerts, and public gatherings. Visitors commonly reach it through nearby Metro and regional rail stations. Its open lawns provide prominent views of the tower and connect several museums and monuments along the Seine.

title: Gustave Eiffel and Nineteenth-Century Structural Design
text: Gustave Eiffel was a French civil engineer known for metal bridges, railway structures, and the Paris tower that bears his name. His company developed methods for prefabricating iron components with precise calculations for wind resistance and load distribution. Eiffel also contributed to the internal framework of the Statue of Liberty. His later scientific work included aerodynamics and meteorological observations conducted from the tower.

title: World Fairs and the 1889 Exposition Universelle
text: The 1889 Exposition Universelle was held in Paris to mark one hundred years since the French Revolution. Nations and companies displayed advances in industry, architecture, science, and culture. The entrance arch built by Gustave Eiffel's company became the event's most enduring structure. Although it was originally authorized as a temporary exhibit, its scientific and communications uses helped preserve it after the exposition.

title: Understanding Atmospheric Pressure
text: Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by the weight of air above a surface. Standard pressure near sea level is approximately 101.325 kilopascals, though weather and elevation cause variation. Pressure influences boiling, weather systems, aviation, and human physiology. Barometers measure atmospheric pressure, while controlled pressure chambers allow researchers and engineers to study environments above and below normal atmospheric conditions.

title: Cooking and Heat Transfer at High Altitude
text: Cooking at high altitude often requires adjusted time and temperature because reduced atmospheric pressure lowers the boiling point of water. Foods cooked by boiling may take longer even though the water begins boiling sooner. Bakers also adjust leavening, liquid, and flour ratios. Pressure cookers compensate by trapping steam and raising internal pressure, allowing water and food to reach temperatures above the ordinary boiling point.

title: Phase Changes in Matter
text: A phase change occurs when matter transitions among solid, liquid, gas, and plasma states. Melting and freezing involve transitions between solid and liquid, while vaporization and condensation connect liquid and gas. During a phase change at constant pressure, energy changes intermolecular organization rather than temperature. The exact transition point depends on pressure, purity, and the intermolecular properties of the substance.

title: Sydney: Australia's Largest Metropolitan Area
text: Sydney is the capital of the state of New South Wales and Australia's largest metropolitan area by population. The city developed around Port Jackson and is internationally recognized for Sydney Harbour, the Sydney Opera House, and the Harbour Bridge. Sydney is a major center for finance, tourism, education, and culture. Australia's national capital, federal parliament, and central government institutions are located in Canberra rather than Sydney.

title: Melbourne and the Federation Era
text: Melbourne is the capital of Victoria and served as the temporary seat of Australia's federal government from 1901 until Parliament moved to Canberra in 1927. The city is known for universities, cultural institutions, sport, and nineteenth-century architecture. Competition between Melbourne and Sydney contributed to the constitutional compromise that placed the permanent national capital in a separate federal territory.

title: Australian Federal Government Institutions
text: Australia is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy with legislative, executive, and judicial institutions. Parliament House in Canberra contains the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Governor-General represents the monarch, while the Prime Minister leads the government. The High Court interprets the Constitution. State and territory governments retain responsibility for many services under Australia's federal system.

title: Chloroplast Structure and Function
text: Chloroplasts are organelles in plants and algae where photosynthesis occurs. Their internal thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll and electron-transport proteins used in light-dependent reactions. The surrounding stroma contains enzymes for the Calvin cycle, which incorporates carbon dioxide into organic molecules. Chloroplasts possess their own DNA and are understood to have evolved from photosynthetic bacteria through endosymbiosis.

title: The Carbon Cycle and Plant Productivity
text: The carbon cycle moves carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, living organisms, soils, and rocks. Plants remove atmospheric carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and store carbon in tissues. Respiration, decomposition, combustion, and ocean exchange return carbon to other reservoirs. Changes in land use and fossil-fuel consumption alter these flows, making plant productivity and ecosystem conservation important components of climate research.

title: Cellular Respiration and Energy Release
text: Cellular respiration is the set of metabolic pathways that releases usable energy from organic molecules. In aerobic organisms, glucose and oxygen are converted into carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. Glycolysis begins in the cytoplasm, while later stages occur mainly in mitochondria. Photosynthesis stores light energy in sugars, whereas cellular respiration makes that stored energy available for cellular work.

title: Earth's Five Oceanic Divisions
text: Earth's connected global ocean is commonly divided into the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic oceans. These divisions reflect geography, currents, climate, and historical convention. The Pacific covers the greatest area, the Atlantic is the second largest, and the Arctic is the smallest. Ocean boundaries are useful for mapping and administration even though seawater circulates continuously among all basins.

title: The Atlantic Ocean and Global Navigation
text: The Atlantic Ocean lies between the Americas and Europe and Africa. It has been central to migration, exploration, trade, conflict, and cultural exchange. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge marks a divergent tectonic boundary running through much of the basin. Major currents such as the Gulf Stream redistribute heat and affect weather and climate on both sides of the ocean.

title: The Mariana Trench
text: The Mariana Trench is a crescent-shaped depression in the western Pacific formed where one tectonic plate descends beneath another. Challenger Deep is its deepest surveyed region and lies nearly eleven kilometers below sea level. The trench experiences immense pressure, low temperatures, and darkness, yet specialized organisms survive there. Research vehicles use reinforced crewed or robotic systems to explore this extreme environment.

title: Document Integrity with SHA-256
text: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function that maps an input of arbitrary length to a fixed 256-bit digest. A small change to a document produces a substantially different digest, making hashes useful for integrity verification. A trusted system can store the digest at ingestion and recompute it before use. Hashing detects modification but does not prove that the original document was truthful, so content validation remains necessary.

title: Indirect Prompt Injection in Retrieval Systems
text: Indirect prompt injection occurs when external content contains instructions that a language model may mistake for trusted commands. In a retrieval system, the malicious instruction can arrive through a document selected for topical relevance. Effective defenses clearly delimit retrieved text as untrusted data, detect imperative or link-based payloads, and restrict the generator to higher-priority system instructions.

title: Hybrid Information Retrieval
text: Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and semantic ranking. BM25 rewards documents containing informative query terms, while dense embeddings retrieve passages with similar meanings even when wording differs. Reciprocal Rank Fusion can merge the two ranked lists without requiring their raw scores to share a scale. The approach is useful for small RAG systems because it balances exact matching with semantic recall.

title: Anomaly Detection in Embedding Space
text: Documents represented as dense vectors can be evaluated relative to a clean reference distribution. Mahalanobis distance incorporates feature covariance, while Isolation Forest estimates how easily an observation can be separated from normal examples. Neither method understands truth by itself. Combining statistical scores with behavioral patterns and query-specific evidence produces a more useful security signal.

title: Zero-Trust Context Processing
text: A zero-trust retrieval pipeline assumes that every external passage may be inaccurate or malicious, regardless of relevance. Each candidate is checked for integrity, scored for suspicious behavior, and either accepted or quarantined. Accepted passages are placed inside an explicitly delimited untrusted-context section. The generator is instructed to use them only as reference information and never execute embedded commands.
